item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face

Published October 29, 2026

Update on GitHub

35

merve

merve

Alvaro Bartolome

alvarobartt

Rémi Ouazan Reboul

ror

Cyril Vallez

cyrilvallez

Quentin Gallouédec

qgallouedec

Enrique Hernández Calabrés

ehcalabres

Juan Julián

juanjucm

Xuan-Son Nguyen

ngxson

Pedro Cuenca

pcuenq

ben burtenshaw

burtenshaw

Aritra Roy Gosthipaty

ariG23498

Mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:

  • FP8
  • NVFP4

There are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

Table of Contents

  • "Welcome Le Chonk: Mistral Large 4 on Hugging Face" Table of Contents What is new with Mistral Large 4 Cybersecurity Capabilities Architecture Vision encoder Benchmark Results Inference Support Transformers vLLM Llama.cpp Fine-tuning with TRL Inference Endpoints Dell Enterprise Hub Try it out

What is new with Mistral Large 4

Mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

Cybersecurity Capabilities

Mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super important for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

For community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Architecture

Mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers. The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

Vision encoder

Mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Benchmark Results

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:

  • Artificial Analysis Cyber Index: ML4 ranks among the top five models globally on this independent evaluation of models’ ability to find and fix software vulnerabilities.
  • Vulnerability reproduction and patching: It achieves 82%, the highest reported score on this test within the index. The task requires reproducing a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patching it, testing both investigation and remediation.
  • Cybench: ML4 solves 93% of a suite of 40 challenges drawn from security competitions, demonstrating strong performance on hands-on security problems.

Mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Inference Support

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

Transformers

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

To run the model, upgrade the transformers package

pip install --upgrade transformers
import os
from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM, DistributedConfig

distributed_config = DistributedConfig(
    tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
    ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]),
)

model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=distributed_config,
)

# only text
text_messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Who are you?"
    }
]

# text + image
multimodal_messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {
                "type": "image",
                "image": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/huggingface/cats-image/resolve/main/cats_image.jpeg",
            },
            {
                "type": "text",
                "text": "How many cats are in the image?",
            },
        ],
    },
]

for messages in [text_messages, multimodal_messages]:
    inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
        messages,
        add_generation_prompt=True,
        tokenize=True,
        return_dict=True,
        return_tensors="pt",
        reasoning_effort="medium",
    ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype)
    input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]

    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=100)
    if int(os.environ["RANK"]) == 0:
        print(processor.decode(outputs[0][input_len:], skip_special_tokens=False))

You can run the script above by saving it in a python file script.py and then run

torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 script.py

vLLM

vLLM supports the high-quality NVFP4 Mistral Large 4 checkpoint, which has a smaller memory footprint and requires NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. The model also ships with a DSpark drafter for additional speed-ups with vLLM. Launch the server like this:

vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
  --config-format mistral \
  --load-format mistral \
  --tensor-parallel-size 8 \
  --decode-context-parallel-size 8 \
  --enable-expert-parallel \
  --dtype bfloat16 \
  --max-model-len 131072 \
  --max-num-seqs 16 \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 2048 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --enforce-eager \
  --mm_processor_cache_gb 0.0

Once the server is up and running, you can run the following.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"What is 17*23?"}],"max_tokens":512}'

Llama.cpp

Llama.cpp and Llama App already support Mistral Large 4.

You can install Llama App with the following command:

curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh

Then you can start the server as follows, indicating the quant suffix after the model ID:

llama serve -hf ggml-org/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-GGUF:Q2_K

Here’s the repository with the quants derived from the FP8 checkpoint, and this is the NVFP4 one, converted from the official NVFP4 repo.

Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat using the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more.

curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "messages": [
            {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."},
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ]
    }'

You can run image-text inference as follows.

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \
    -d '{
        "model": "muse-spark-open",
        "messages": [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": [
                    {
                        "type": "text",
                        "text": "What is in this image?"
                    },
                    {
                        "type": "image_url",
                        "image_url": {
                            "url": "data:image/png;base64,..."
                        }
                    }
                ]
            }
        ],
        "temperature": 0
    }'

The llama.cpp team ships the following quants: IQ2_XXS, Q2_K, Q4_K_M, NVFP4, Q8_0, and BF16 for further conversions. The 2-bit quants run on a single Apple Silicon Ultra computer with 512 GB of unified RAM. The others require distributed inference. You can also run on multiple NVIDIA or AMD cards.

Running Q2_K on a single M3 Ultra, we got a prefill throughput of about 90 tokens per second, and a generation speed of 15 tok/s. On 4 x RTX6000 Pro, we observed the following results:

  • NVFP4: 32K context size, prefill 130-590 t/s, gen speed ~10 t/s
  • IQ2_XXS: 800K context size. At short context sizes, prefill is 500 tok/s and generation runs at 30 tok/s. However, using long contexts performance drops to 129 tok/s (prefill) and 3 tok/s (generation).

Fine-tuning with TRL

We also ship day 0 support of fine tuning Mistral Large 4 using TRL. All you have to do is upgrade to the latest version of transformers, trl and peft.

pip install --upgrade transformers trl peft

In the following example we train the model to perform multilingual thinking. The fine tuned model would be able to reason in the language the system prompt asks for!

The script runs on the FP8 variant on a node of 8xB300s. The full example, with a Slurm launcher, is in TRL's examples.

# torchrun --nproc-per-node 8 sft.py
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, DistributedConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

world_size = int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"])
model_id = "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B"
model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    distributed_config=DistributedConfig(fsdp_size=world_size, ep_size=world_size),
    dtype="auto",
)

dataset = load_dataset("HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking", split="train")
# the assistant turns carry reasoning, so render them in reasoning mode
dataset = dataset.map(lambda x: {"chat_template_kwargs": {"reasoning_effort": "high"}})

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=model,
    args=SFTConfig(
        packing=True,
        max_length=4096,
        assistant_only_loss=True,
        learning_rate=1e-4,
        lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
        warmup_steps=10,
    ),
    train_dataset=dataset,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(
        r=16,
        lora_alpha=32,
        target_modules=r".*language_model.*\.(q_proj|kv_a_proj_with_mqa|kv_b_proj|o_proj|gate_proj|up_proj|down_proj)",
    ),
)
trainer.train()

Inference Endpoints

Mistral Large 4 is also available on Inference Endpoints, with a ready-to-deploy recipe on 8 x NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The recipe runs vLLM with the FP8 weights split across all eight GPUs using tensor and expert parallelism, and uses the model's built-in DSpark draft head for faster generation through speculative decoding. It serves up to 131K tokens of context and processes up to 16 requests at a time, and we observed the following results:

  • Single request: time to first token of about 0.6 seconds for a 1K-token prompt, and a generation speed of ~65 tok/s, reaching 120–138 tok/s on chat prompts where DSpark's drafts are accepted.
  • Long prompts: 16K-token prompts, four at a time, are prefilled at about 4,300 tok/s in total, with a time to first token of 8–9 seconds.
  • Under load: about 480 tok/s of total generation across 1,000 ShareGPT conversations.

You can deploy it with the hf CLI as follows:

hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B --name mistral-large-4

Once the endpoint is running, you can query its OpenAI-compatible API, using the endpoint URL and your Hugging Face token. The reasoning_effort field controls how much the model reasons before answering, and can be set to low, medium, or high (default).

curl "$(hf endpoints describe mistral-large-4 --json | jq -r .status.url)/v1/chat/completions" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $(hf auth token 2>/dev/null)" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
        "model": "mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B",
        "messages": [
            {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"}
        ],
        "reasoning_effort": "medium"
    }'

The answer comes back in choices[0].message.content, and the reasoning in choices[0].message.reasoning. The endpoint also supports tool calls, structured outputs, image inputs, and streaming through the standard Chat Completions fields.

Dell Enterprise Hub

The easiest way to get up and running with your Dell AI Servers (NVIDIA H200, B200, GB200 or GB300) is by installing the dell-ai CLI:

pip install dell-ai && dell-ai login

And use it to run an optimized recipe for Mistral Large 4 on e.g., a NVIDIA B300 node.

dell-ai models deploy --model-id mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B-NVFP4 \
    --engine docker \
    --platform-id xe9780-nvidia-b300 \
    --gpus 4

You can find more about this release in the Dell Enterprise Hub (DEH).

Try it out

Grab the weights from the Mistral Large 4 collection, run them locally with the GGUFs, or deploy them with Inference Endpoints. We can't wait to see what you build with Le Chonk. Share your fine-tunes, quants and other artefacts on the Hub!

item.description: Full title: Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

Introducing AnySpeechRecognizer and AnyDecisionModel: Open Models for Speech and Decisions on Apple Platforms

Published October 29, 2026

Update on GitHub

8

Mattt

mattt

Language models can do a lot. They write, summarize, translate, and call tools. But they're only a small part of what machine learning can do.

Say a customer calls your support line. First, you want to know what they said (speech recognition). Then, you want to decide where to send them (decision). You could hand both to a language model, but there are models built for each that are better, faster, and less expensive.

In our AnyLanguageModel 1.0 recap, we looked at a year of local and hosted models in Swift. With AnyLanguageModel and swift-huggingface now on their 1.x releases, we're extending the same approach to speech and decisions: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of model.

Today we're announcing two packages:

  • AnySpeechRecognizer implements Apple's new speech-to-text API with a choice of recognition engine, including NVIDIA's Parakeet and Alibaba's Qwen3-ASR running locally on Core ML, and adds speaker diarization to track who speaks when.
  • AnyDecisionModel answers yes-or-no, multiple-choice, and rating-scale questions with typed results and probabilities. It derives each answer from the model's probabilities instead of generating text, using a model on your device with MLX, Core AI, or llama.cpp, or a decision model from Jev or Ollama.

Both packages can download open models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them on device.

AnySpeechRecognizer

Computers have been transcribing speech for decades, and in the past few years, they've gotten very good at it. Apple platforms already have an API for it. macOS 26 and iOS 26 introduced SpeechAnalyzer, Apple's new speech-to-text API. You add modules such as SpeechTranscriber and SpeechDetector to an analyzer, give it a file or a stream of audio buffers, and read results from async sequences as they arrive. AssetInventory installs the models, so your app decides when downloads happen.

It's a well-designed API, but the only engine behind it is Apple's. AnySpeechRecognizer keeps the API and lets you choose the engine:

- import Speech
+ import AnySpeechRecognizer

The package mirrors SpeechAnalyzer, SpeechTranscriber, DictationTranscriber, SpeechDetector, and AssetInventory, with Apple's Speech framework as the default engine. If your code uses that shared API, changing the import is enough. To use Parakeet instead, change only how you create the transcriber:

let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: ParakeetSpeechModel(variant: .v3),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [.volatileResults],
    attributeOptions: [.audioTimeRange]
)

The steps for installing assets, running the analyzer, and reading results stay the same. The README has a complete example and lists the differences from Apple's framework.

Meet the models

Parakeet v3 is NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3. It's a polyglot: it recognizes 25 European languages and works out which one it's hearing, so you don't pass a locale.

Parakeet Ultra is Moondream's post-trained take on v3. It was more accurate in most of our measurements.

Parakeet Unified is NVIDIA's English-only Parakeet.

All three Parakeets run on the package's own Core ML runtime, which supports file and live input, volatile results, word timing, and word confidence.

Qwen3-ASR is Alibaba's speech model, in 0.6B and 1.7B sizes. It recognizes 30 languages and 22 Chinese dialects, including Mandarin, Cantonese, Japanese, and Korean, which Parakeet doesn't cover. It detects the language automatically, or you can set one:

let transcriber = SpeechTranscriber(
    model: QwenSpeechModel(variant: .large, language: Locale.Language(identifier: "yue")),
    transcriptionOptions: [],
    reportingOptions: [],
    attributeOptions: []
)

Qwen3-ASR gives one final result for each segment of up to 40 seconds, without volatile results, word timing, or confidence. It runs on the GPU and is slower than Parakeet, so it's better suited to transcribing files than live input.

To add another engine, implement SpeechRecognitionModel for its configuration and SpeechRecognitionExecutor for one module's session. The README includes a small provider that reports placeholder text to help you get started.

Core ML models on the Hub

To run these models in apps, we converted them to Core ML and published them on the Hub:

ModelCore ML conversionOriginal checkpointLicense
Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3mattt/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3-coremlnvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3CC BY 4.0
Parakeet Ultramattt/parakeet-ultra-coremlmoondream/parakeet-ultraCC BY 4.0
Parakeet Unified EN 0.6Bmattt/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-coremlnvidia/parakeet-unified-en-0.6bNVIDIA Open Model License
Qwen3-ASR 0.6Bmattt/qwen3-asr-0.6b-coremlQwen/Qwen3-ASR-0.6B-hfApache 2.0
Qwen3-ASR 1.7Bmattt/qwen3-asr-1.7b-coremlQwen/Qwen3-ASR-1.7B-hfApache 2.0
Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2-coremlnvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2CC BY 4.0
Streaming Sortformer 4spk v2.1mattt/diar-streaming-sortformer-4spk-v2.1-coremlnvidia/diar_streaming_sortformer_4spk-v2.1NVIDIA Open Model License

Each repository records its source checkpoint and a checksum for every file, and the package pins it to a fixed revision. The Parakeet repositories add an 8-second encoder for live input, which cuts live analysis time by about a third at the cost of a somewhat higher word error rate. The repository also has the conversion workflows, most of which follow FluidInference's mobius scripts, and checks each conversion against the original model.

Downloads happen only when your app asks for them: about 600 MB for each Parakeet, plus about 590 MB for the live encoder, 0.9 to 2.4 GB for Qwen3-ASR, and about 250 MB for Sortformer. Files go in the standard Hugging Face cache, so a Mac app outside the sandbox shares them with Python and other Hugging Face tools.

Speaker diarization

When you transcribe a conversation, you often want to know who said what. That's speaker diarization, and Apple's Speech framework doesn't have a module for it, so AnySpeechRecognizer adds one. SpeakerDiarizer runs NVIDIA's Streaming Sortformer on Core ML alongside an Apple or Parakeet transcriber, on the same timeline:

let diarizer = SpeakerDiarizer(model: SortformerDiarizationModel())
if let request = try await AssetInventory.assetInstallationRequest(
    supporting: [transcriber, diarizer]
) {
    try await request.downloadAndInstall()
}
let analyzer = SpeechAnalyzer(modules: [transcriber, diarizer])

The diarizer tracks up to four speakers, even when they talk over each other. A SpeakerTimeline collects its results and attributes each timed word to a speaker, so you can print a transcript by speaker turn. Like image support in AnyLanguageModel, this goes beyond what Apple's API offers today.

The diarizer uses Sortformer v2 by default. You can also choose v2.1, which NVIDIA trained with more meeting data and which was more accurate on meetings in our measurements, too.

How well does it work?

We measured the package with its hear command-line tool on an M4 Max Mac Studio with macOS 27.0.1. Here are the word error rates on LibriSpeech files of 3 to 8 minutes:

Transcribertest-cleantest-other
Parakeet v3, file1.55%2.78%
Parakeet v3, live4.73%4.29%
Parakeet Ultra, file1.66%2.55%
Parakeet Ultra, live2.65%3.28%
Parakeet Unified, file1.43%2.19%
Parakeet Unified, live1.45%2.42%
Apple's transcriber, file2.12%3.97%

Parakeet transcribes an hour of audio in about 20 to 40 seconds from a file, or about 1.5 to 2.5 minutes live, with about 100 MB of memory once Core ML has compiled the model. Qwen3-ASR is much slower and needs a few gigabytes of memory. Meetings are hard for everyone: on AMI recordings, where people talk over each other, every engine we tested had a word error rate above 23%.

These numbers come from one machine and a few datasets, so measure with your own hardware and audio. hear evaluate works on your own files, and the repository's natural-speech-eval.py tool reproduces these measurements. So far, we've tested only on macOS 27, not on an iPhone.

Next, we'd like to add more engines, including Core AI on macOS 27 and iOS 27.

AnyDecisionModel

AnyDecisionModel is a different story. There's no Apple framework to map onto, and decision models aren't new, exactly.

It's only a decision model if it comes from the Décision region of France;
otherwise, it's sparkling zero-shot classification.

What's new is the name, a lot of hype, and a crop of models trained to make decisions. We think that's where things are going, so we wanted a Swift API that's ready for them.

Apps often ask language models to make decisions. Is this message urgent? Which team should handle this ticket? How frustrated is this customer? The usual approach is to prompt a language model and parse the text that it generates. That gives you one answer, but doesn't show the probabilities it assigned to the alternatives.

Here's what a decision looks like in Swift:

import AnyDecisionModel

enum Department: String, Choosable {
    case billing, technical, sales
}

let ticket = "I was charged twice for my order, and now the app logs me out when I try to ask for a refund."

let model = MLXDecisionModel(modelID: "mlx-community/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-4bit")
let session = DecisionSession(model: model, state: .text(ticket))

let urgent = try await session.probability(of: "Does this convey urgency?")
let team = try await session.choice("Which team?", from: Department.self)
let anger = try await session.score(
    "How frustrated?",
    levels: ["Calm", "Frustrated", "Very angry"]
)

urgent is a Double. team is a Choice<Department> containing the selected case, a probability for each option, and a confidence value. anger is a Score containing the expected level, a probability for each level, and a confidence value. Because Department conforms to Choosable, team.value is a Department that you can use in an exhaustive switch.

If you've used Foundation Models or AnyLanguageModel, the model-and-session pattern will look familiar. A DecisionSession holds a single state, which can be text or JSON, and every question is about that state. Questions are independent: an answer never becomes input to a later question. To ask several questions at once, pass them to decide(_:) as a batch.

For each question, the MLX backend builds a prompt with a one-token label for each allowed answer, then reads the probability of each label from one forward pass.

Try it out: Emoji Magnet

Emoji Magnet is a macOS app with a text field above a pile of 343 emoji. Type a phrase, such as "things you wear", and the emoji that match rise out of the pile. Refine it to "things you wear in winter", and the emoji that no longer match fall back.

The app has no built-in keyword rules; the model decides everything at inference time. When you pause typing, it asks the model one yes-or-no question for each emoji, for example:

Statement: a heavy winter coat fits the description "things you wear". Is this statement true?

The session's state holds the phrase. The demo above uses the hosted Jev backend, which answers all 343 questions in one request, so the emoji settle in about half a second for each phrase. Without a TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, the app runs Qwen3 4B on your Mac with the MLX backend. That backend uses prefix caching to evaluate the state once, then answers 16 questions per forward pass. On an M4 Max, a group of 16 takes about 0.45 seconds after the model loads. A full pass over all 343 emoji takes about 10 seconds, and each group's results appear as soon as they arrive.

Emoji Magnet is in the AnyDecisionModel-Examples repository.

Decision heads and Clef

Reading next-token probabilities works with general-purpose language models, but those models weren't trained to make decisions. Cloudflare's Clef models are an example of a newer approach: a model with a trained decision head that turns a state and a schema of typed questions into decisions, returning probabilities for all allowed options across the questions in one forward pass. Clef-Flash is the 9B variant.

AnyDecisionModel runs Clef-Flash on a Mac with MLX:

let model = MLXHeadDecisionModel(
    modelID: "mlx-community/clef-flash-4bit",
    head: .jointSchema
)

You use the same sessions and questions, but MLXHeadDecisionModel reads each decision from Clef's trained decision head instead of from next-token probabilities. The 4-bit model is a 6.2 GB download, and its model card recommends a Mac with at least 16 GB of memory. Clef can read images and video, but this backend accepts only text and JSON states.

Calibrating and checking probabilities

Raw probabilities from language models are often overconfident. The local backends accept a Calibration, which applies a temperature to every answer and a bias to yes-or-no answers. Use separate datasets to fit the calibration and evaluate the results.

Language models can also favor an option because of its position in a list. On the MLX, Core AI, and llama.cpp next-token backends, turn on rotationDebiasing to ask a choice question once for each rotation of the options and average the probabilities. That costs one prompt evaluation per rotation.

Each local choice and score also includes a confidence value based on the entropy of its probabilities. It measures how concentrated the probabilities are, not whether the answer is right, so check the error rate on your own data before you pick a threshold. The next-token backends' diagnostics report how much probability the model assigned to the allowed answers. A low value means it assigned most of the probability elsewhere.

Backends

AnyDecisionModel has six backends:

  • MLX runs a small language model on Apple silicon with mlx-swift-lm and downloads it from the Hub.
  • MLX decision heads run a model with its own trained decision head, such as Clef.
  • Core AI does the same as MLX with a Core AI model on macOS 27 and iOS 27.
  • llama.cpp reads decisions from a local GGUF model through llama.swift.
  • Jev calls TypeSafe's Jev through the System One API, or any server that implements it, such as Kev.
  • Ollama calls a System One decision model on a local Ollama server or in Ollama's cloud. It requires Ollama 0.35.0 or later, or 0.40.5 or later for cloud models.

The next-token backends label answers "yes" and "no", A to Z, or 0 to 9, so a choice can have at most 26 options, and a score at most 10 levels. Decision heads have no such limit.

Like AnyLanguageModel, the package uses Swift package traits. Without traits, it has no third-party dependencies. You get the core types and the Jev and Ollama backends, which also build on Linux. Enable the MLX, CoreAI, or Llama trait for the local backends.

Get started

Both packages require Swift 6.2 or later and macOS 26 or iOS 26 or later. The Parakeet and Sortformer runtimes and the MLX backend require Apple silicon. AnyDecisionModel's MLX build tasks use Xcode's Swift 6.4 or later and the Metal toolchain; Core AI requires Xcode 27 and an OS 27 runtime.

Add the packages to your Package.swift:

dependencies: [
    .package(url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnySpeechRecognizer", from: "0.1.0"),
    .package(
        url: "https://github.com/mattt/AnyDecisionModel",
        from: "0.6.0",
        traits: ["MLX"]
    ),
]

For now, AnyDecisionModel's CoreAI trait can't be combined with AnySpeechRecognizer, because coreai-kit 0.7.3 requires swift-huggingface below 1.0 and AnySpeechRecognizer requires 1.x.

Each README has more examples and details about requirements and backends. AnySpeechRecognizer also includes a command-line tool, hear, that transcribes local files, labels their speakers, and evaluates the results. Every hear command requires --backend apple, --backend parakeet, or --backend qwen; run hear prepare with the same backend and model options before analysis to install the needed assets.

Try them in your apps and tell us what works and what doesn't. Issues and pull requests are welcome on both repositories.

Links

  • AnySpeechRecognizer on GitHub
  • AnyDecisionModel on GitHub
  • AnyDecisionModel-Examples on GitHub
  • AnyLanguageModel on GitHub
  • swift-huggingface on GitHub

Thanks to NVIDIA for Parakeet, Sortformer, and NeMo, to Moondream for Parakeet Ultra, to FluidInference, whose FluidAudio and mobius projects documented the conventions that the Parakeet runtime and the Core ML conversions follow, to Cloudflare for Clef, and to everyone who contributed to AnyLanguageModel, whose patterns both packages borrow.

item.description: Full title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
item.content:encoded:
Back to Articles

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt

Enterprise + Article

Published October 28, 2026

51

Maryam Motamedi

maryameee

nvidia

Piotr Żelasko

piotrzelasko

nvidia

Kunal Dhawan

kunaldhawan

nvidia

Nikolay Karpov

nkarpov

nvidia

Nune Tadevosyan

nunetadevosyan

nvidia

Meline Mkrtchyan

mmkrtchyan

nvidia

Nithin Rao Koluguri

nithinraok

nvidia

Francesco

fciannella

nvidia

One open model for multilingual transcription, speaker attribution, translation, and audio Q&A, with top leaderboard results, plus the open Granary v2 data pipeline and fine-tuning recipes to adapt it.

A transcript can capture every spoken word and still leave users or applications wondering who said what, how to translate it, or how to format domain-specific jargon. Multilingual calls, fast-paced meetings, and medical dictation each need different output: a translation, speaker labels, or correctly spelled medical terms.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe is an open-weight, promptable model that turns recorded speech into useful text, now available on Hugging Face and ModelScope. It brings transcription, speaker attribution (diarization), translation, and audio question answering into one checkpoint: it transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers. Developers can guide output with natural language, choose where their audio is processed, and adapt recognition to domain vocabulary and accents.

Transcribe is first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English and sits on Artificial Analysis’s accuracy–active-parameter frontier. For speaker attribution, it posts the lowest error rate on David AI’s 21-language diarization leaderboard and ranks first in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison. Quantized versions are coming soon, so you can run Transcribe locally on your RTX Spark, DGX Spark, or Jetson AGX Thor—or scale up on Blackwell data-center GPUs.

Granary v2’s multilingual data (available on Hugging Face and ModelScope) and reusable curation pipeline, together with NeMo Speech fine-tuning tools, extend prompt-level control to training: developers can define the written form they need and adapt the model to the speech their applications encounter. In a medical case study, fine-tuning cut word error rate (WER) on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt.

Guide transcription and analysis with natural language

The same checkpoint can turn one meeting recording into different outputs, depending on the instruction:

  • “Transcribe this recording and label each speaker.”
  • “Translate this audio into English.”
  • “What decisions were made in this meeting?”

Experience the model in action in the video below, where it tackles a classic scene from the 1940 screwball comedy His Girl Friday—a film famous for its rapid-fire, heavily overlapping dialogue.

Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe captions a scene from His Girl Friday (1940) and labels speakers, including overlapping dialogue.

For unfamiliar terms, try context before training. In a healthcare setting, for example:

Transcribe this medical discussion in the original language. Possible terms: HbA1c, metformin. Use these terms only when supported by the audio. Preserve standard medical spelling and write numbers in conventional written form.

The model card has recommended presets, including reasoning for audio questions, plus the full prompt guide and a task-by-language matrix: language support differs by task, and audio question answering is trained in English. Word-level timestamps are also supported. As with any speech model, spot-check names, speaker changes, and answers against the recording.

From live classes to lasting lessons. Agora, whose real-time voice and video platform powers live conversations in apps, used word-level timestamps in a classroom demo: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe turns a recorded class into a transcript shown alongside the replay, so students can see what was said and when. Agora’s blog walks through how they built it.

Leaderboard wins from transcription to speaker attribution

Among open-weight models, Transcribe leads on what was said; on who said it, it tops two speaker-attribution benchmarks outright.

Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard. The leaderboard measures transcription accuracy as word error rate (WER) on public test sets, in three tracks:

  • English: first among open-weight models at 5.33% average WER (Figure 1).
  • Multilingual: 4.62% mean WER across seven languages, the lowest among evaluated open-weight models in the model card’s Open ASR comparison.
  • Long-form: 10.98% mean WER, also the lowest in that comparison.

Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard (English) at 5.33% average WER, with API models excluded. Lower WER means fewer transcription errors.

Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Text Leaderboard. Artificial Analysis independently ranks speech-to-text models by AA-WER, its word error rate index. Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe ties for first among open-weight models at 2.8% AA-WER, with about 4B active parameters versus 24B for the model it ties. On AA-AgentTalk, the held-out voice-agent speech set that makes up 50% of the AA-WER index, Transcribe scores 1.8% WER, versus 2.3% for the next-best open-weight model. Transcribe pairs its speech encoder with a hybrid Mamba–Transformer mixture-of-experts language model, so only about 4B of its 30B parameters are active per token. That puts it on Artificial Analysis’s open-weight Pareto frontier of accuracy versus active parameters. On AA’s all-model chart, it ranks ahead of several widely used proprietary speech APIs.

Figure 2. Leading AA accuracy at about one-sixth the active parameters: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe achieves 2.80% AA-WER with approximately 4B active parameters.

Speaker attribution across languages and overlap. Sortformer speaker cues reach the language model with the acoustic features, so Transcribe can tag each turn during generation instead of relying solely on a later step to attach speakers to words.

David AI DAI-ASR-I18N Leaderboard. On David AI’s DAI-ASR-I18N combined transcription-and-speaker-attribution track, Transcribe ranks first among evaluated open-weight models and second overall. On the benchmark’s diarization track, which scores who spoke when across 21 languages, it has the lowest diarization error rate of the 14 systems tested, slightly ahead of NVIDIA’s dedicated Nemotron 3 Diarization model.

Figure 3. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots on David AI’s multilingual diarization leaderboard: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe posts the lowest overall diarization error rate (DER), 18.26% across 21 languages, followed by Nemotron 3 Diarization at 18.38%. DER measures speaker-time errors; lower is better.

VoiceArena Diarization-Bench. On VoiceArena’s English full-session benchmark, Transcribe posts the lowest concatenated minimum-permutation WER (cpWER) of 14 systems and ranks first in both in-person and online settings. It also drops the fewest words: deletions are 8.32% of reference words, versus a median of about 31%.

Figure 4. NVIDIA models hold the top two spots in VoiceArena’s 14-system comparison: Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe leads at 32.4% cpWER, followed by NVIDIA Multitalker Parakeet with Nemotron 3 Diarization at 34.2%. Diarization-Bench v1 covers English full sessions, overlapping speech and 2–8 speakers. cpWER counts word errors after matching speaker labels; lower is better.

More evaluations. Ocular AI’s Converse-STT evaluation ranks Transcribe the top open model. Josh Talks’ Voice of India leaderboard reports Transcribe’s results across Indian languages.

High-throughput transcription. In benchmarking, Transcribe processed 100 hours of audio in under three minutes on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, using the forthcoming NVFP4 quantized version. Results were measured on 30-second clips at high concurrency.

Serve the available checkpoint with vLLM today. Local deployment with NeMo-Speech.cpp is coming soon alongside the quantized versions. Transcribe is built for recorded audio, not live streaming.

Specialized recordings can still call for adaptation to domain vocabulary and transcript conventions. Granary v2 and NeMo Speech fine-tuning address that, starting with the data behind Transcribe.

Granary v2: The open data curation pipeline behind Transcribe

A promptable speech model requires training data with unambiguous formatting targets. Granary v2 is part of the Nemotron speech collection on Hugging Face and ModelScope. Built with NVIDIA NeMo Curator, its reusable pipeline prepared multilingual speech used in Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe’s training, producing aligned transcript variants, task labels, and inspectable quality metadata. The public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in Granary v1. These figures describe the dataset release, not Transcribe’s full training mixture or its sampling weights.

Granary v2 generates three transcript forms for each recording (Table 1), the same verbatim and clean styles developers can request from Transcribe with a prompt. Beyond transcription, the pipeline produces short audio captions, code-switching restoration of loanwords, speech-grounded Q&A pairs, contextual ASR biasing terms, and translations with automatic quality scores.

Training targetIllustrative transcript
Text-normalized, verbatimI paid, uh, twenty-five euros.
Inverse text normalization, with disfluenciesI paid, uh, €25.
Inverse text normalization, without disfluenciesI paid €25.

Table 1. Granary v2 training targets for the same utterance.

The pipeline is organized into four reusable stages:

  • 1. Audio Preparation (Metadata): Segments raw or long-form audio, tracks speakers across the full recording, and tags acoustic events and language. Granary v2’s sources were already segmented, so this release skipped this stage.
  • 2. Transcription (ASR): Routes each language to primary and recovery ASR models, falling back when the primary fails a hallucination check. Human reference transcripts help preserve trusted spellings while adding spoken forms and disfluencies.
  • 3. Task Label Generation (Text): Derives transcript variants, then checks character rate, hallucination patterns, and model or human-reference agreement. Only accepted records receive contextual-ASR terms and translations.
  • 4. High Fidelity (HiFi): Filters out segments that are noisy, clipped, or contain multiple speakers, keeping a smaller set of high-quality recordings for uses beyond ASR. For the VoxPopuli dataset, it reduced 354k hours to 111k hours across 22 European languages.

Figure 6. Granary v2 data curation pipeline, following one sample from raw audio through the Metadata, ASR, and Text stages to a training example.

Developers can run the NeMo Curator pipeline with Ray and NVIDIA Dynamo backends on their own recordings or authorized public corpora, or build on the Granary v2 public manifests. The manifests include the three transcript forms as tn_raw, itn_raw, and itn_clean, the labels described above, entity hints, derived instruction pairs, provenance, and a per-record quality flag. Download source audio separately under each corpus’s original license, and follow the release’s published terms.

Adapt recognition to the vocabulary that matters

Start with a development-set prompt that specifies language, script, and transcript format. In the case study below, naming English and the Latin alphabet in the prompt cut full-benchmark WER from 30.8% to 23.8%. For domain errors that remain, the NeMo Speech fine-tuning workflow pairs representative speech with explicit written targets.

The NeMo Speech medical ASR case study shows this progression on Eka Care’s open benchmark of recordings from Indian doctors and medical students, which has 3,619 clips and no designated training split. The study builds adaptation data from generated medical text and public medicine catalogs, then combines approximately 153 hours of synthetic speech, 29 hours of accented English from Common Voice, and 63 hours of medical recordings from MultiMed.

Figure 7. On the full test set of Eka Care’s Indian medical speech benchmark, a better prompt cuts WER from 30.8% to 23.8%, and fine-tuning brings it to 11.8%, about 62% fewer transcription errors than the model out of the box. The full set includes the 855 tuning clips used to choose the prompt and checkpoints; the held-out results below are the cleaner test.

Synthetic generation separates the written target from its spoken rendering: “HbA1c” is the label, while “H B A one C” is sent to the synthesizer. Multiple TTS voices broaden the audio; real recordings add accents and recording conditions. Training text is filtered for exact matches and shared eight-word sequences with benchmark references.

As with Granary v2’s explicit targets, training examples vary digits, unit spacing, company-name expansion, and brand-name hyphens, with instructions specifying the required convention. Some prompts include term lists with near-miss distractors, so the model learns to use a spelling only when the audio supports it. The final system uses one fixed convention prompt and one model pass, without retrieval or transcript post-processing.

The recipe trains the speech encoder and projection and uses LoRA to adapt the language model. Two runs use different data mixtures; after adapter merging, selected checkpoints are uniformly averaged into one final model. Checkpoint selection uses decoded development-set results, rather than training loss alone. The full adaptation, from text generation through evaluation, took about 14 GPU-hours on one NVIDIA GB300.

Domain gains, measured on held-out speakers

The study splits the benchmark by speaker into 855 tuning clips, used to choose the prompt and checkpoints, and 2,764 held-out clips, decoded once per final system. Using Eka Care’s KARMA scoring pipeline, fine-tuning cuts held-out WER from 22.44% for the best-prompt baseline to 12.17%, a 45.8% relative reduction and the clearest evidence that the gains generalize to new speakers. Keyword WER falls from 9.2% to 6.5%, and semantic WER from 10.0% to 7.6%. On the same held-out speakers and scorer, the adapted model’s 12.17% WER beats an open medical-specialist model (13.79%) and a widely used general-purpose ASR model (14.92%).

On general English, LibriSpeech test-clean WER rises slightly, from 1.54% to 1.69%. The medical specialist still leads on exact matches for brand-name drugs and diagnostics; the study points to real recordings of clinicians saying brand names as the next step. For your own domain, keep at least 100 real, labeled clips for checkpoint selection, and evaluate the entity types your application depends on alongside general-speech retention.

The case study includes commands to reproduce each step. The fine-tuning tutorials cover recipes, resource requirements, and tools for training, export, and evaluation, including new-language and code-switching ASR. The accompanying agent skill lets a coding agent run the workflow, from baseline selection and data checks through training validation, adapter merging, and evaluation.

ModelScope also enables developers to fine-tune Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe through its ms-swift framework for specialized multimodal applications.

Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2

Try Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe in the Hugging Face demo or on ModelScope Studios, then download the checkpoint from Hugging Face or ModelScope. For self-hosted transcription, get started with vLLM or SGLang-Omni, both offering support from day one.

To skip self-hosting, use a hosted endpoint from Baseten, DeepInfra, or Simplismart.

To adapt it to your domain, start with the Granary v2 manifests on Hugging Face or ModelScope and the medical ASR case study, or let a coding agent drive the workflow with the fine-tuning agent skill.

Models & Datasets

  • Model Checkpoints: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on Hugging Face, ModelScope | Interactive Demo on Hugging Face, ModelScope
  • Hosted Endpoints: Baseten, DeepInfra
  • Dataset Manifests: Granary v2 Manifests on Hugging Face, ModelScope
  • High Fidelity Subset: Manifests on Hugging Face, ModelScope | Space on Hugging Face

Repositories & Tutorials: NVIDIA NeMo Speech GitHub | NeMo Curator Granary v2 Pipeline | vLLM Deployment Guide | Speech Fine-Tuning Guide | Fine-Tuning Agent Skill

Partner Blogs: Agora | Inflection AI | VoiceArena | Simplismart | DeepInfra

LiquidAI

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

  • More capability per parameter: a new tri-hybrid architecture and training recipe allow LFM3-1.7B to outperform LFM2.5-2.6B while using 35% fewer parameters.
  • Every modality on one backbone: six 2B-class models (text, vision, audio, omni, and decision) trained from LFM3-1.7B-Base, including our first omni model and video input for our vision model.
  • Built for the edge: the text model fits in about 1 GB at 4-bit precision, new in-house vision and audio encoders speed up processing, and the text model’s 256K context window lets agents run on-device.
  • Made to be specialized: every model fine-tunes on a single GPU, so you can adapt it to your data, terminology, and deployment environment.

How we built a more expressive backbone

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

  • Tri-hybrid layer mix: 13 gated short convolutions, 5 sliding-window attention (SWA) layers with a 256-token window, and 6 global attention layers. The convolutions use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.
  • Head-wise gated attention: a sigmoid gate scales each head's output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization.
  • Partial RoPE: global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head, so the other half matches on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.
  • Sandwich norm: each block normalizes both its input and its output to keep activations well-scaled.

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

One backbone for six models

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

ModelInputOutputBuilt on
LFM3-1.7BTextTextLFM3-1.7B-Base
LFM3-VL-2BText, images, videoTextLFM3 backbone + vision encoder
LFM3-Audio-2BText, audioText, speechLFM3 backbone + audio encoder, audio decoder, and LiquidCodec
LFM3-Omni-2BText, images, video, audioText, speechLFM3 backbone + vision and audio encoders and audio decoder
d1-2BText, images, videoCalibrated answersLFM3-VL-2B
d1-omni-2BText, images, video, audioCalibrated answersLFM3-Omni-2B

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

  • Vision encoder: it combines convolution and attention and uses 3x less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B's vision encoder in accuracy while requiring 2.2x fewer FLOPs (both measured with the same LFM2.5-230M language backbone). For video, it embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice, halving the temporal sequence length.
  • Audio encoder and LiquidCodec: the audio encoder mixes sliding-window attention and short convolutions and is fully causal, so the model can prefill while you speak, with time to first token as low as 50 ms. LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, turns generated tokens into speech at about 87x real time on a single CPU thread on Apple M4 Max and supports streaming decoding.

How to use the LFM3 models

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

LFM3-1.7B

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

pip install -U transformers

Then load and run the model:

from transformers import pipeline

generator = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model="LiquidAI/LFM3-1.7B",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "What is C. elegans?"}]
output = generator(
    messages,
    do_sample=True,
    temperature=0.1,
    top_k=50,
    repetition_penalty=1.1,
    max_new_tokens=2048,
)
print(output[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

LFM3-VL-2B

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.21.0" torch torchvision pillow

Then load and run the model:

import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForImageTextToText, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-VL-2B"

model = AutoModelForImageTextToText.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True)
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)

messages = [
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "url": "https://placecats.com/300/200"},
            {"type": "text", "text": "Describe this image."},
        ],
    }
]

inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    messages,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)

with torch.inference_mode():
    output_ids = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        do_sample=True,
        temperature=0.1,
        top_k=50,
        repetition_penalty=1.1,
        max_new_tokens=16384,  # generate() needs an explicit limit; reasoning can be long
    )

generated_ids = output_ids[:, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :]
print(processor.batch_decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

LFM3-Audio-2B

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch accelerate librosa soundfile

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

import torch
import soundfile as sf

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Audio-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

conversation = [
    {"role": "system", "content": "Respond with interleaved text and audio."},
    {"role": "user", "content": [{"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"}]},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": "<|mixed_start|>"},
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    continue_final_message=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(
        **inputs,
        max_new_tokens=1024,
        audio_temperature=1.0,
        audio_top_k=128,
        audio_repetition_penalty=1.1,
        audio_repetition_window=4096,
        return_dict_in_generate=True,
    )

    text = processor.decode(
        outputs.sequences[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:],
        skip_special_tokens=True,
    )
    waveform = codec.decode(
        outputs.audio_codes[:1, :, :outputs.audio_lengths[0]]
    ).audio_values[0]  # 24 kHz
print(text)
sf.write("reply.wav", waveform.float().cpu().numpy(), 24_000)

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

LFM3-Omni-2B

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.20.2" torch torchvision torchcodec accelerate pillow librosa soundfile
import torch
import soundfile as sf

from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor

model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM3-Omni-2B"
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.bfloat16 if device == "cuda" else torch.float32

model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id, dtype=dtype, device_map=device, trust_remote_code=True
).eval()
processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
codec = processor.audio_tokenizer.to(device=device).eval()

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

conversation = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": "Answer questions about the provided image. Base every answer only on what can be seen. Respond with text.",
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [
            {"type": "image", "image": "photo.jpg"},
            {"type": "audio", "audio": "question.wav"},
        ],
    },
]
inputs = processor.apply_chat_template(
    conversation,
    add_generation_prompt=True,
    tokenize=True,
    return_dict=True,
    return_tensors="pt",
).to(device)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, generation_mode="text")

print(processor.decode(
    outputs.sequences[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:outputs.sequence_lengths[0]],
    skip_special_tokens=True,
))

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

d1-2B and d1-omni-2B

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

Between the two d1 models:

  • d1-2B: choose it for text, pictures, and video. It replaces d1-3B with a third fewer parameters and scores higher on all four of our decision suites, for example, 75.5 against 64.0 on ImajevBench.
  • d1-omni-2B: choose it when your inputs include audio. If you ask by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

pip install "transformers>=5.19" torch torchvision pillow

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu"
dtype = torch.float32 if device == "cpu" else torch.bfloat16
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("LiquidAI/d1-2B", trust_remote_code=True, dtype=dtype).to(device)

# Several named questions over one state, answered in one pass
questions = {
    "refund": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Is the customer asking for a refund?"},  # yes/no: P(yes)
    "team": {"type": "choice", "instructions": "Which team should handle this?",
             "criteria": {"billing": "Charges, refunds, invoices", "shipping": "Delivery and parcels",
                          "technical": "App or site faults"}},
    "topics": {"type": "choice", "multiple": True, "instructions": "Which topics does the message raise?",
               "criteria": {"billing": "Payments and charges", "delivery": "Shipping and parcels",
                            "login": "Signing in to the account"}},
    "urgency": {"type": "score", "instructions": "How urgent is this ticket?", "criteria": ["low", "medium", "high"]},
}
out = model.system_one("I was charged twice and my parcel never arrived. Please refund one charge.", questions)
a = out["answers"]
urgency = a["urgency"]["legend"][str(int(a["urgency"]["score"]))]
print(round(a["refund"]["noul"], 2), a["team"]["choice"], a["topics"]["choices"], urgency)
# 1.0 billing ['billing', 'delivery'] medium

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

Fine-tune LFM3 for your task

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

ModelMethodTaskNotebook
LFM3-1.7BSFTExtract structured JSON from messy documentsOpen in Colab
LFM3-1.7BDPOAnswer from retrieved documents, or declineOpen in Colab
LFM3-1.7BGRPOCall the right tools in a 108-tool phone appOpen in Colab
LFM3-1.7BCPTLearn a new language (Turkish) from raw textOpen in Colab
LFM3-VL-2BSFTRead receipt photos into JSONOpen in Colab
LFM3-VL-2BGRPOTranscribe images of equations to LaTeXOpen in Colab
LFM3-Audio-2BSFTMap spoken smart-home commands to function callsOpen in Colab
LFM3-Audio-2BSFTTeach the model a new voiceOpen in Colab
LFM3-Omni-2BSFTMap spoken smart-home commands to function callsOpen in Colab
LFM3-Omni-2BSFTAnswer spoken questions about medical imagesOpen in Colab

Example: teaching LFM3 to act

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

Get Started with LFM3

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

  • Download: the LFM3 collection on Hugging Face, including LFM3-1.7B-Base for your own post-training.
  • Fine-tune: adapt LFM3 to your task with our fine-tuning notebooks.
  • Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi.

We can't wait to see what you build.
